title: RagnaDuds - Ragnarok Online Server
description: A rathena server built for friends split between Denmark and Brazil. Multi-arch Docker images on an ARM cloud VM, a patched and translated 32 bit game client, installers for Windows and Linux, and a retro website with live server stats. You can check it live [here](https://ragnaduds.duckdns.org)!
content:
Ragnarok Online was the game of my childhood. My friends are now spread between Denmark and Brazil, which is a terrible setup for nostalgia, so instead of hunting for a public server we could all agree on, I built us our own. Two of them actually, one for the classic pre-renewal era we played as kids and one for the modern renewal era, plus a website, installers for Windows and Linux, and a small command line tool so I can run the whole thing from my kitchen table.

It is friends only and non commercial. Honestly, the game part was never the hard part. What kept me busy for weeks was everything around it, the infrastructure, the packaging, and a frankly unreasonable amount of reverse engineering on a client that was compiled when I was still in school.

![Prontera, the capital, rendered by the browser client](/images/ragnaduds-prontera.mp4)

## How it runs

Everything lives on one ARM VM from Oracle Cloud, twelve containers behind a single compose file. rathena, the open source C++ emulator, needs three processes per server (login, char, map), plus a small web api that newer clients expect, plus its own MariaDB. Two eras, so double all of that, then Caddy in front and a status sidecar watching both.

::flow ragnaduds

Three decisions made the rest of the project boring in the good way, which is exactly what I want from something I maintain on a Tuesday night.

- **Images are built once on my PC**, for amd64 and arm64, then pushed to a private registry. The VM never sees a line of source code, it only pulls.
- **Configs never go into an image or into git.** Each host has its own folder with secrets, rates, game scripts, mounted at runtime. Changing a drop rate needs no rebuild.
- **The databases have no public port.** Only the game containers and the sidecar reach them, over internal docker networks.

![The stack running on my machine, from the same compose file as the VM](/images/ragnaduds-docker.png)

## The command center

One Bash script wraps all of it. I wrote it because I got tired of remembering which flag went where at one in the morning, and it ended up being the piece I use the most.

- `release` builds multi arch, pushes, tags both latest and the git sha, so a rollback is a tag change instead of a rebuild
- `up vm` rsyncs the configs, pulls, recreates only what actually changed, warns me first if somebody is playing right now
- `start` and `stop` run only the era we picked for that night
- `accounts` applies the local accounts file over ssh as idempotent SQL
- `package` and `files` build the client zips and upload them resumably
- `backup` pulls database dumps down to my PC, with a cron on the VM keeping seven days

::flow ragnaduds-release

## The client was the hard part

The server is a modern codebase. You compile it, you move on. The client is a 32 bit Windows program from another era, running under Wine for me and natively for my friends, and it very much does not want to talk to anything it was not born to talk to.

The exe build date has to match the server packet version exactly, so I picked a 2021 Korean exe for the classic server, a 2026 one for renewal, then compiled each server for its date. Both exes went through **WARP**, an open source patcher, to read local files before the game archives, drop the anti cheat, point at our address. Those patch sessions are version controlled like everything else. Along the way I wrote a small Python reader for the GRF archive format so I could actually see what the client was loading instead of guessing.

::flow ragnaduds-client

The one I am proud of is the item table. The 2026 exe only ever loads a single compiled Lua file full of Korean names, and the English translation just sits in the same folder being politely ignored. So that file became a tiny loader that runs the original bytecode, overlays the English table on top of it, then appends our custom items. Testing it meant building a **32 bit Lua container**, because the bytecode is 32 bit and nothing modern would even parse it. Twenty seven thousand items load in half a second.

The cash shop bug was more fun to hunt. The first item showed the right price, the second one showed 544194803. The exe had been patched to expect item preview data in every shop entry, the server was not sending it, so every entry after the first was read out of alignment. One compile flag in the Dockerfile fixed it, with rathena's source untouched.

## Bringing a dead server back

Brazil's official server shut down in 2026 and my Brazilian friends would not stop talking about its events. So I went digging in the Wayback Machine, found the old announcements, matched Portuguese monster names to ids through community databases, and rebuilt three of them.

- **Mapas Especiais**, eight rooms with instant respawn and no experience loss
- **Cheffenia**, an MVP arena with doubled boss HP and a thousand kill daily fatigue
- **Turn In**, a hunting quest

The special maps are shared instances, private copies of existing maps reachable only through the event NPCs, so the normal world stays untouched and the client needs no change at all. The buff NPC stands on the exact town coordinates the old server used. Nobody asked for that detail, everybody noticed it.

![Mapas Especiais, Turn In and Cheffenia, live on the local server](/images/ragnaduds-events.mp4)

## A casino, played with zeny

Comodo has a casino hall in the original game, so I filled it. A hostess in Prontera takes you inside, and both floors now have working tables. Everything is played with zeny, the in game money, never with real money.

- **Blackjack** with a fresh six deck shoe every hand, a dealer who stands on all 17s, doubles and splits, and blackjack paying 3 to 2
- **Roulette** on two tables
- **Ten slot machines** sharing one progressive jackpot
- **A daily lottery** with tickets, where 70% of the sales go into the pot and the draw runs every evening
- **Jogo do Bicho**, Brazil's famous animal game. It started in 1892 as a raffle to keep a zoo in Rio de Janeiro open, and it has been illegal since the 1940s, yet you still find it on street corners all over the country. Twenty five animals each own four numbers, there are five draws a day, and you can bet on the animal or on the last two, three or all four digits of the winning number.

Every game is animated with art and sounds made by two small Python scripts, and the odds are tuned like the real thing, about 94% back on the slots, 97% on roulette and 99.5% on blackjack. The money is settled before the animation plays, so closing the game in the middle of a spin never eats a win.

![Roulette, slots, Jogo do Bicho, the lottery and blackjack, the real animation frames players see](/images/ragnaduds-casino.mp4)

## The website

A single static page, no framework, deliberately ugly in the way 2004 was ugly. Pixel font, CRT scanlines, the works.

- A **login page** with the same username and password as the game, and Caddy checks with the account portal before it serves any page
- **Live status** from the sidecar, whether each world is online and who is playing
- A **Hall of Fame** with the top ten by MVP kills and by PvP kills, the PvP counter coming from a small server script I wrote for it
- A **mini game** with my face on a knight sprite fighting an orc, ragdoll physics through matter.js
- A **collage** of my photo with game art on physics springs, backgrounds cut out with rembg, laid out with Pillow
- **Three languages**, EN, PT and DA, guessed from the browser and remembered

The Hall of Fame turned out to be the best thing on the whole site, not because it was hard, but because my friends now check it before they log in.

![Scrolling the site](/images/ragnaduds-website.mp4)

## Accounts, requests and email

The server is still friends only, but nobody has to message me for an account anymore. A small **account portal**, one Go binary with SQLite behind Caddy, takes care of it.

- Anyone can **request to join** on the website. They read the terms, confirm the project has no connection with Gravity, pick a username and leave a message if they want. The request then waits for me.
- Nothing is created until **I approve it**. Approving creates the game account on both servers at once and emails a link to choose a password. Rejecting can send a polite email as well.
- The same username and password open both the **website and the game**. Players can change their password from their account page, and a forgotten one gets a reset link that works once, for two hours.
- **Email** goes out over SMTP through the server's own Gmail account, and every message is also kept in an outbox page for me. Instead of a ping per request, I get one short daily summary when someone is waiting.

## Installers

Each download ships a Windows or a Linux installer. Both unpack the game, check every file against a manifest (sizes, plus the exe hash), confirm the client points at our server, test that the server answers, then create the shortcuts.

- **Windows**, PowerShell with WinForms, restyled to match the site. It has to stay ASCII only, because Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads scripts in the ANSI code page and a single accented character breaks the whole thing.
- **Linux**, Python with a GTK window that falls back to Tk, then zenity, then a plain terminal. Each install gets its own Wine prefix. It works on Fedora, which is what we run, and it knows Debian and Ubuntu need 32 bit Wine enabled first.
- The zips also carry a self hunting homunculus AI, so my friends do not need the external tools we all used as kids.

![The Linux installer halfway through unpacking the game](/images/ragnaduds-installer.jpg)

## Playing in the browser

Installing a 32 bit Windows game is still a small project of its own, so the newest piece is a **browser client**. Both worlds can be played straight from the website, behind the same login, with nothing to install.

- The client is **roBrowserLegacy**, an open source Ragnarok client written in JavaScript and WebGL, pinned to a tested commit with a few patches of my own on top.
- Browsers cannot open raw TCP connections, so a small **WebSocket proxy** runs next to it on the VM and forwards the game traffic to login, char and map, the same packets the desktop client sends. It only talks to our three game servers and only accepts pages from our own site.
- The game files are built from the **same downloads** my friends install, the same archives in the same order, the same music and the same item list, so both clients always match.
- Renewal needed two fixes. Its 2026 archives start with a different header, "Event Horizon" instead of "Master of Magic", so the file server had to learn to accept it, and the custom cash shop needed the same item preview fields as the desktop exe.

The browser does all the drawing. The server only moves files and game packets, exactly like it does for the installed game.

![Yeah, that's me in North Vietnam, close to China, ragnarokized](/images/ragnaduds-browser-login.jpg)

## Bugs worth telling

- **The server banned itself.** Before accounts existed, the char server kept dropping the map server, which reconnected many times per second, until rathena's anti flood guard banned our own container. Fixed by trusting the internal docker network.
- **A 5 GB installer crash.** PowerShell picked the integer overload of a Max call, and 5,140,330,802 bytes does not fit in an int. I reproduced the exact error message in a PowerShell container before touching the real installer, then moved it to doubles.
- **Commands did nothing.** rathena's commands aimed at other players start with a hash, but the 2026 client silently drops any chat line starting with one. So the command symbol became an exclamation mark.
- **Error loading data account settings.** Newer clients keep per account settings on a separate web service, and the translation pointed it at localhost. That is why rathena's web server shows up twice in the architecture diagram.

## What I learned

- **Legacy software is archaeology.** Version matching, byte patterns, reading archive formats nobody documents anymore. That was half the project.
- **Separating images from config** makes a tiny deployment feel professional. Releases, rollbacks, config changes, all of them are one boring command.
- **Test on the real target.** A 32 bit Lua runtime, Windows PowerShell 5.1, a clean Debian container. Almost every bug only showed itself there.
- **Nostalgia is a great project manager.** I would never have finished this for a client, but I finished it for friends who wanted to hunt Porings again.

Ragnarok Online is a trademark of Gravity Co., Ltd. This is a non commercial fan project for friends, not affiliated with Gravity, and no game files are distributed publicly.

::callout You are welcome to join [here](https://ragnaduds.duckdns.org/join)!

title: CS Duds 1.6 in the browser
description: Self hosted Counter-Strike 1.6 that runs in a browser tab, with no install and no Steam account. The real engine compiled to WebAssembly, a Go backend for the lobby and a WebRTC relay to one game server per room, ten modes and about 300 maps, all from one docker compose command.
content:
Counter-Strike 1.6 came out in 2003 and somehow it still refuses to die. Playing it today usually means Steam accounts, installs and somebody renting a server. So I made it boring. You open a link, you pick a room, you play. In a browser tab, with no install, no plugin and no Steam account.

It is all self hosted. One docker compose command on a Linux machine gives you a lobby, a game server per room and the whole game served to the browser. And the game is the real thing, the actual Half-Life engine running in WebAssembly, talking to a real Counter-Strike server. I did not rewrite Counter-Strike. I just convinced it to live somewhere it was never meant to live.

![Hard bots on de_dust2, watched in first person from the spectator seat, in a Chrome tab](/images/csduds-dust2.mp4)

## How it works

Three moving parts. **Caddy** hands out the page and the game files. A single **Go backend** runs the lobby API and a WebRTC relay. Behind it sits one plain **Counter-Strike server per room**, started and stopped on demand.

::flow cs-duds

The interesting bit is the network. The game speaks UDP, and browsers are not allowed to open raw UDP sockets. So the packets had to take a detour.

- The browser opens **one WebRTC data channel** to the Go backend, unordered and with no retries. That is about as close to UDP as a browser gets, so the game feels like a normal client.
- I replaced the engine's own send and receive calls with a few lines of JavaScript, so every packet the engine sends goes into that channel instead of a socket.
- The engine believes it is connected to 192.0.2.1, an address reserved for documentation. The relay knows which room you actually meant.
- **The relay can never be an open proxy.** No address ever travels on the wire. The only thing a client picks is a room id, and only live rooms resolve.
- Every player gets **their own local address** on the server side, somewhere in 127.10.x.y. The server builds each player's id from their address, and without that trick everybody would be the same person, which is funny for about one round.

## The lobby

The front page is a small TypeScript app with no framework. Quick play buttons per mode, a server list with search, filters and a card view, a players page, and a page to create a server.

- **Quick play** joins the fullest open server of that mode, or starts one if there is none.
- **Names are unique.** Your browser claims a name with a random token, so nobody else can play under it.
- **Invite links** drop a friend straight into your room.

![The lobby with a few rooms running, the card view, server details and the players page](/images/csduds-lobby.mp4)

## Creating a room

Ten modes. Classic, deathmatch, free for all, GunGame, zombie, aim, AWP, knife, surf and climb. Pick one, search a map, pick a room size, open the advanced settings if you care, and create.

- The map list follows the mode. Surf maps only show up for surf, knife maps only for knife, and so on.
- **Advanced settings come from a small JSON file per mode.** Deathmatch offers the kill announcer, spawn protection and the flashlight. The backend checks every value against that file before the server ever sees it.
- Creating a room does not join it. You get a toast with the invite link and a join button, so the host can send the link first.

![Creating a deathmatch room on de_dust2 for eight players](/images/csduds-create.mp4)

A room is just a game server process on its own port. The number of ports in the config is the number of rooms, which is the cheapest capacity planning I have ever done.

::flow cs-duds-room

## Joining

Clicking join does three things behind a loading screen. It downloads what is missing, boots the engine, and connects through the relay.

- The game files are packed at build time into **one base bundle and one bundle per map**. The browser downloads the base once, then each map the first time it needs it.
- Everything is **checked with sha256** and kept in the browser's cache, so the next visit skips the download.
- The team picker lives **outside the game**, in the page, using the game's own character art converted for the web. Picking a team is a click, and that click is what lets the page grab the mouse.

![From the join button to the first steps on de_dust2, after adding ten hard bots. The wait while joining is cut short](/images/csduds-join.mp4)

The host gets controls in the overlay. Kick players, add bots by team and difficulty, start a map vote, or close the server. Everybody else can still vote with rtv and /votekick in the chat.

![The overlay, one Esc away. Host controls, bots and the map vote](/images/csduds-overlay.jpg)

## Maps

About 300 maps. The stock ones, community maps from a CS 1.6 server mirror pinned to one git commit, and a list of extra maps from **GameBanana**. Yes, that includes Chaves and the Simpsons. Some things are not negotiable.

- The GameBanana maps are too big for git, so a small Python script fetches them once per machine. It unpacks every archive inside a throwaway container and keeps only map files, never anything that could run.
- **Every map is checked at build time.** A Go tool reads each map and makes sure every texture and model it needs is really there. A broken community map is quietly left out. A missing sound or sky is fine.
- File names are lowercased, because the Linux server opens files case sensitively and map makers on Windows never had to care.
- My favourite fix. One of the Chaves maps wants Half-Life's potted plant under a different file name. So the build copies the original plant from the server files and renames it. A whole map, held hostage by a plant.

![fy_simpsons_house from GameBanana, purple stairs and pink car included, same spectator view](/images/csduds-simpsons.mp4)

## Plugins and sounds

The servers run ReHLDS, ReGameDLL, Metamod-R, ReUnion and AMX Mod X. **ReUnion** is the piece that lets players in without Steam. On top of that I wrote a few small AMX Mod X plugins.

- **Kill announcer** with the classic Unreal style voices. First blood, headshot, multi kill, killing spree, all the way to godlike. The sounds ship in the browser's base bundle, so the server only has to say which one to play.
- **Zombie mode.** Fifteen seconds into each round one random player turns into a zombie, and every hit infects a human.
- **Climb timer** for KZ maps, from the start button to the end button.
- **Chat votes** for rtv and /votekick. Chat text never reaches a server command. Maps come from the map cycle and kicks go by user id.
- **Navigation builder.** Random spawns need the bots' navigation file, which most maps do not ship. So on a new map the plugin adds one helper bot, lets it build the file, then kicks it. It happens once per map and the file is kept in a Docker volume.
- **GunGame** is compiled from its source during the build, with its sounds pinned like everything else.

## The engine, compiled from source

The browser runs **Xash3D FWGS** with **cs16-client**, both compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten. They are git submodules pinned to one commit each. I never use prebuilt engine files. FWGS themselves warn that third party builds often carry malware, and they publish no browser build of their own.

Upstream's browser build is old, so it needs small fixes. Each one is a short patch in the repo, twelve in total, so every change to upstream code can be read on its own.

- The engine runs one endless loop, which a browser tab will happily freeze on forever. One patch hands each frame to the browser's animation loop instead.
- Another one asks for WebGL 2, and another stops the engine from popping a browser alert when a map is missing, so the page can recover on its own.
- Dependabot proposes submodule updates once a week. I read the upstream changes, check the patches still apply and the tests pass, then merge.

## Building and running it

The whole thing is one Dockerfile with thirteen stages and two final images, one for the backend and one for Caddy. Both run on the host network, so the relay, the game servers and the per player addresses all share one loopback.

::flow cs-duds-build

- **Every download is pinned.** One text file lists each third party download with its URL and sha256. A wrong hash fails the build. Base images are pinned by digest.
- **Configuration is an env file** where every key is optional. Room ports, idle timeout, rate limits, the admin password hash.
- **Tests at three levels.** Go unit and API tests, tests against the real running stack, and Playwright tests that open real browsers, join rooms and check that two players actually see each other.

## Bugs worth telling

- **Particles were culled wrong.** cs16-client defined GL_PROJECTION_MATRIX as 0x0BA1. That number is actually GL_NORMALIZE. The real one is 0x0BA7. One character, one patch.
- **The bots froze the server.** Building a map's navigation makes the bot code block the whole server for a while. My backend saw a server that stopped answering and killed the room. Now a room gets two full minutes of silence before it counts as hung.
- **Ctrl+W closed the game.** Crouch is Ctrl, walk forward is W, and in a browser that combination closes the tab. In fullscreen the page now locks the keyboard, so every key goes to the game. Outside fullscreen it asks before the tab closes.
- **SteamCMD needs convincing.** Downloading the server files fails a few times with "Missing configuration" before it works. The build now retries until SteamCMD literally prints that the game is fully installed.
- **Big community maps ran out of memory**, with an error that says "greater then free hunk", typo included. The server now starts with a bigger heap.

## What I learned

- **The browser can do far more than I thought.** WebAssembly, WebGL 2 and WebRTC together run an engine from the Half-Life era at a smooth frame rate on an integrated Intel GPU, with nothing installed.
- **WebRTC is not only for video calls.** An unreliable data channel is a perfectly good UDP tunnel, and pion makes the server side pleasant in Go.
- **Pin everything, check everything.** Hashes on every download and a checker on every map turned a lot of surprises into build errors.
- **Small patches beat a fork.** Twelve short, readable patches on top of upstream are much easier to keep alive than my own copy of an engine.

A legal note, because it matters. The server software and the browser engine are open source, but the Counter-Strike game files belong to Valve, and serving them to browsers counts as redistribution. So CS Duds is for private use with friends, behind an unlisted link or a password, never a public site.

::callout The code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/dudustri/cs-duds-manager). Bring your own friends, the bots are already included.

title: rustboy-color GBC emulator
description: A Game Boy Color emulator written in Rust. One core with zero dependencies runs as a desktop app on x86_64 and aarch64 and in the browser through WebAssembly. The CPU passes Blargg's test ROMs, the screen draws one pixel at a time, and it plays games.
content:
I always wanted to know what actually happens inside a Game Boy. Not the marketing version, the real one. Which wire is busy, which chip waits for which, why a game can change the scroll halfway down the screen and get away with it. Reading about it only got me so far, so I decided to build one. In Rust, from scratch, with the Pan Docs open in another tab at all times.

rustboy-color is a Game Boy Color emulator. The same core runs as a desktop app on x86_64 and aarch64 and in a browser tab through WebAssembly. The CPU is done, the screen is done, cartridges and saves work, and it plays games. Right now I am teaching it to make noise.

![The title screen, running in the browser. A photo turned into 160 by 144 pixels at compile time](/images/rustboy-splash.mp4)

## One core, two homes

The whole project rests on one rule. **rustboy-core never touches the outside world.** It does not open files, read the clock, start threads or draw anything. It has zero dependencies. You give it a game, ask for a frame, and get a picture back. Everything that differs between a laptop and a browser lives in a host crate on top.

::flow rustboy-crates

- **rustboy-core** is the console. CPU, screen, sound chip, timer, buttons, cartridge.
- **rustboy-frontend** is the loop both apps share, so the browser cannot drift from the desktop. A platform only has to say how to tell the time, where to paint and how to show it.
- **rustboy-splash** is the title screen. A build script crops, recolours and shrinks a photo when the crate compiles, so the browser only ever receives raw pixels and no image library.
- **rustboy-desktop** is a winit window drawing through pixels, 640 by 576, paced at 59.73 frames a second.
- **rustboy-wasm** is the browser host, plus a tiny file server written with nothing but the standard library so I can try it locally.

## Time moves four ticks at a time

The real hardware takes no turns. The CPU, the screen and the timer all move on the same clock edge. Code can only do one thing at a time, so the question is how big a turn should be.

The easy answer is one whole instruction per turn. I went the other way. Every memory read or write moves the entire machine forward four ticks first, then the value arrives. Nobody writes down that an instruction takes 12 cycles. It just falls out of counting the memory accesses it makes, exactly like on the chip.

::flow rustboy-loop

It is more work per instruction, and it is the one decision in the project that would be painful to undo. But it means the screen and the timer see the world change in the middle of an instruction, which is exactly where the timing tests like to poke. A frame is 70,224 ticks, and the loop does not even count them. It just runs the CPU until the screen says the picture is done, which stays right when the Color switches its CPU to double speed.

## The CPU

The Game Boy runs a Sharp SM83, a cousin of the Z80 and the 8080. I wrote all of its roughly 500 instructions as small steps, one memory access at a time, with interrupts, HALT, STOP, the delay after EI and the famous HALT bug, where the CPU forgets to move on and reads the same byte twice. The 11 empty opcode slots lock up a real Game Boy, so mine refuses them loudly instead of guessing.

The flags live as four plain booleans and only become a byte when something asks for the F register. Easier to read, and much easier to get right.

## The screen

This was the biggest part, and the most fun. A Game Boy has nowhere near enough memory to keep a whole picture around, so it builds the picture while the screen is showing it, one pixel per tick, left to right. I copied that instead of drawing a whole line at once.

- A **background fetcher** in five steps feeds a queue of pixels, and a mixer takes one pixel out every tick
- The **window** layer with its own line counter, and **sprites** with the ten per line limit, flips, priority and six extra dots for every sprite fetched
- **Colour** for real, eight palettes for the background and eight for sprites, two banks of video memory, and per tile palettes and flips
- **DMA** for copying sprites in one go and for the Color's bulk and line by line video copies
- **Video memory is locked** while a line is being drawn, because on the hardware that wire is physically busy and games rely on it

The nice side effect is that the drawing time of a line comes out on its own. Sprites and the window stall the fetcher, so the line takes longer, so the gap after it gets shorter. A whole line approach would have to fake that number.

## Cartridges and saves

A cartridge can hold megabytes, but the CPU only sees 32 KB of it at a time. A small chip on the cart, the MBC, swaps which 16 KB slice shows up. rustboy-color handles **MBC1, MBC3 with its real time clock, and MBC5**, and it refuses a header whose checksum does not add up.

Saves leave the core as plain bytes and each host decides where they go. On desktop a .sav file sits next to the game, written beside it and then swapped in, so a crash halfway cannot shred an old save. In the browser it goes into localStorage. A game writes its save many times a second, so the frontend waits a second after the first write and then stores it in one go.

## Test ROMs

Blargg's test ROMs run on a real Game Boy and compare every instruction against it. The two that matter most for the CPU run in CI on every pull request, on x86_64 and on aarch64, and the job fails if the ROMs are missing instead of quietly skipping them.

![cpu_instrs in the browser, all eleven groups passing. Sped up four times](/images/rustboy-cpu-instrs.mp4)

I ran the whole Blargg collection for this page. The full workspace has **292 tests passing**, and the ROMs land like this.

- **cpu_instrs**, all 11 groups pass
- **instr_timing** passes
- **mem_timing**, both versions, 3 of 3
- **halt_bug** passes
- **interrupt_time** still fails, it is on the list
- **oam_bug**, 2 of 8. That one checks a memory corruption quirk of the original grey Game Boy, which I have not copied
- **dmg_sound** 0 of 12 and **cgb_sound** 1 of 12, which is fair, the sound chip is the thing I am building right now

![Six Blargg results, straight from the core's framebuffer](/images/rustboy-test-roms.png)

## In the browser

wasm-pack turns the browser crate into about 160 KB of WebAssembly plus the JavaScript that loads it. The canvas is the console's real size, 160 by 144, and CSS stretches it with pixelated scaling, so it looks crisp on any screen. Every animation frame the frontend runs one console frame, copies the pixels into an ImageData and puts it on the canvas. You pick a game with a normal file input and it never leaves your machine.

Controls are the same on both versions.

- **Arrows** for the d-pad
- **A** and **X** for the A and B buttons
- **Enter** for Start and **Shift** for Select
- **F11** for fullscreen and **Esc** to quit, desktop only

## What was hard

- **Discipline more than difficulty.** Writing every instruction as memory accesses is not hard, but doing it 500 times without cheating once is.
- **The last line of the screen lies.** On line 153 the line counter shows 153 for only four ticks and then reads 0, while the comparison behind it keeps seeing 153 a little longer. There is a unit test just for that.
- **Interrupts fire on an edge, not a level.** The screen's STAT interrupt only fires when its line rises. Fire it every time the line is merely high and it goes off far more often than the hardware ever would.
- **Bank masks fail silently.** A wrong mask on a bank number does not crash. It just reads the wrong slice of the game, or worse, the wrong part of your save.

## What I learned

- **Pick the expensive decision early.** Tick by tick timing was the one thing I could not change later, so I paid for it on day one and everything else got easier.
- **A core with no dependencies is a gift.** WebAssembly, ARM, unit tests, all of them were free, because the console never asked anyone for anything.
- **Test ROMs are the best reviewers I ever had.** They do not care how clean the code looks, only whether it does what the chip does.
- **Write it down first.** Every part has a plain language doc in the repo, written before the code. Explaining a chip in simple words is the fastest way to find out I do not understand it yet.

## What is next

Sound. The core already has both square wave channels with their sweep, length and volume envelope, the drawn wave channel and the noise channel, all turning into samples at 48,000 a second. What is missing is the mixer, the panning, and the last step to the speakers, cpal on desktop and WebAudio in the browser. After that come save states and a little debug overlay with a tile viewer.

::callout The source is on [GitHub](https://github.com/dudustri/rustboy-color), and sound is coming soon!

title: Personal Blog & Portfolio
description: This very site. A statically exported Next.js app with an interactive resume, a 3D travel globe, an activity tracker, physics banners and a JSON-driven blog.
content:
This is the source of the site you are looking at right now.

## Stack

Built with Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4 and Bun as the runtime, exported to fully static HTML.

## Features

- Interactive resume with a career timeline and detail cards
- Portfolio tiles with per-project write-ups
- Blog with individual post pages
- A 3D travel globe built on three-globe
- A sports tracker with an activity log and pizza-earned charts
- Gravity and cursor-trail physics banners
- A contact form wired to a Cloudflare Worker with Turnstile

## Architecture

Content lives as JSON, is read through typed data modules, and feeds the App Router pages and their client components. Everything is prerendered to static files at build time.

::flow blog-architecture
